Course Guide

Freight Brokerage & Truck Dispatching

Everything that moves a load from the first phone call to a signed proof of delivery — the people, the equipment, the paperwork, and the rules of the road. Eight modules and a full glossary, at your own pace.

01Truck Drivers & Their Operations12 min ▸ 02Stakeholders in the Trucking Business11 min ▸ 03The Tractor: Anatomy of a Truck10 min ▸ 04Freight Types14 min ▸ 05Load Security & Procedures11 min ▸ 06Safety & Compliance16 min ▸ 07Endorsements, Permits & Legal Documents15 min ▸ 08ELD & The Update Department10 min ▸

This course is built for anyone stepping into a dispatch desk or a brokerage seat — no trucking background assumed. You’ll learn the language of the industry, how a load actually moves, and what keeps a carrier legal and paid.

AHow this course works

Each module on the route to the left stands on its own, but they’re ordered to build on each other: who’s involved, what they drive, what they haul, how it’s secured, how it’s kept legal, and how you keep everyone updated. Click any stop to jump in. Your spot on the route fills in as you go (it resets when you reload).

Self-paced

Go in any order

Follow the route start to finish, or jump straight to the module you need.

Reference

Keep the glossary open

Over 100 working terms, searchable. New word on a load? Look it up.

On the job

Built from real workflow

Rates, paperwork, compliance, and the update process dispatchers run every day.

BWho you’ll be in this business

A dispatcher finds loads, negotiates rates, books carriers, and keeps the load moving on time. A freight broker sits between the company that needs something shipped and the carrier that hauls it. Both live and die by clear communication, clean paperwork, and knowing the rules cold — which is exactly what’s ahead.

New: listen as you learn

Every module has Piper narration — press play in the bar at the top to hear it read aloud, follow the two-line live transcript at the bottom (it scrolls on long modules), and change the speed. Use the moon/sun button (top right) to switch between day and night themes, and click any diagram or photo to zoom it.

Module 1 of 8 · ~12 min
Exit 01

Truck Drivers & Their Operations

Who’s actually behind the wheel, how they’re paid, and the license that lets them drive.

Before you can dispatch a truck, you need to understand the person driving it — how they got there, how they earn, and what their day looks like. It shapes every rate conversation you’ll have.

1.1The trade-offs of life on the road

Trucking is one of the few careers with a genuinely low barrier to entry and strong job security — but it asks a lot in return.

The upside

Why people choose it

Easy start. No degree needed — a CDL and a short course gets you rolling. Job security. Demand for drivers stays high. Independence. No desk, no boss over your shoulder; you set your own rhythm on the road.

The reality

What it costs

Lifestyle. Food on the road is often fast food; staying healthy takes effort. Fatigue. Long hours mean sleep and rest have to be managed carefully. Isolation. It’s mostly a solo job — rewarding for some, lonely for others.

1.2Three ways to drive

Every driver fits one of three business arrangements. Knowing which one you’re talking to tells you how much room there is to negotiate.

Most freedom

Owner-Operator

Owns the truck and runs the business. Keeps more revenue and isn’t subject to forced dispatch — but carries all the risk, expenses, and responsibility.

Middle ground

Lease Operator

Drives a truck leased from a carrier and pays its costs (payments, fuel, repairs, fuel tax). The appeal is “instant ownership” with a small down payment.

Most stability

Company Driver

An employee paid per mile in the company’s truck. Less upside, but no ownership burdens — the company handles the truck, maintenance, and the next load.

Dispatcher takeaway

An owner-operator feels every dollar of a rate and every empty mile — expect harder negotiation. A company driver is on forced dispatch and is paid roughly $0.50–$0.75 per mile regardless.

1.3Solo vs. team — and what a week earns

A solo driver runs alone; a team is two drivers who alternate driving and resting, so the truck almost never stops. Teams cost more but cover far more miles — ideal for expedited, long-distance freight.

Driver typeSolo (weekly)Team (weekly)
Owner-Operator$8,000+ gross$12,000+ gross
Lease Operator$8,000+ gross$12,000+ gross
Company Driver2,500–3,000 mi6,000–6,500 mi

Gross is the total revenue from the loads a truck completes in a week. For a company driver, pay is figured from miles run rather than load revenue.

What a week can look like (illustrative)

Here’s how a solo owner-operator’s week might add up across five loads — the gross is simply the sum of what each load pays:

DayLaneMilesLoad pays
MonRichmond, VA → Atlanta, GA530$1,250
TueAtlanta, GA → Nashville, TN250$700
WedNashville, TN → Dallas, TX660$1,500
FriDallas, TX → Memphis, TN450$1,050
SatMemphis, TN → Richmond, VA820$1,800
Weekly gross2,710$6,300

Reading the week

From that gross, an owner-operator still pays fuel, the truck payment, insurance, maintenance, and tolls — so gross is not take-home. A company driver, by contrast, would be paid on the ~2,710 miles run, not the $6,300 the loads brought in. The numbers here are illustrative, to show the math — not fixed rates.

1.4The CDL: license classes

A Commercial Driver’s License (CDL) is required to operate commercial vehicles over 26,000 lbs. There are three classes, and the class dictates what a driver may legally pull.

ClassWhat it coversVehicles you may drive
Class AAny combination with a gross combination weight rating (GVWR) of 26,001+ lbs, where the towed unit is over 10,000 lbs.Tractor-trailers (18-wheelers), truck-and-trailer combos, tankers, livestock carriers, flatbeds.
Class BA single vehicle 26,001+ lbs not hitched to a heavy trailer.Straight trucks, large buses, box/delivery trucks, dump trucks with small trailers.
Class CVehicles under 26,001 lbs that carry hazmat or 16+ passengers.Doubles/triples, buses, tank trucks, HazMat vehicles (with endorsements).

1.5Getting a CDL

The path is regulated by the FMCSA. The headline steps:

  1. Meet the age rule

    21+ for interstate driving (18+ for intrastate only).

  2. Complete approved training

    For Class A or B, finish training with an FMCSA-approved provider.

  3. Apply & verify identity

    Submit the state CDL application, pay fees, and provide SSN, identity, and residency proof.

  4. Pass the medical & knowledge exams

    Submit a Medical Examiner’s Certificate, pass the vision and knowledge tests, and receive a Commercial Learner’s Permit (CLP).

  5. Wait, then test on the road

    Hold the CLP at least 14 days, then pass the pre-trip inspection and road-skills exam (in your own vehicle) to be issued the CDL.

1.6Documents & places you’ll hear about

Identity

Social Security Number

A nine-digit identifier used to track covered wages and benefits. Created in 1935; issued by the Social Security Administration via Form SS-5.

Licensing

DMV

The Department of Motor Vehicles handles vehicle registration and driver licensing — usually at the state level in the U.S.

On the road

Truck Stops

Establishments for fueling, servicing, repairing, and parking heavy commercial vehicles — plus accessories and a place to rest.

Stakeholders in the Trucking Business

The players on every load — and how the freight and the money flow between them.

A single load can touch four or five businesses before it’s delivered. Knowing each role — and who pays whom — is the foundation of brokering and dispatching.

2.1The main players

Owns the freight

Customer · Shipper / Receiver

The party that owns or needs the freight moved. The shipper sends it; the receiver (consignee) takes delivery.

Arranges it

Broker

The intermediary between shipper and carrier. Brokers manage the logistics and connect freight to trucks.

Hauls it

Carrier

The asset-based company with the trucks and trailers that physically moves freight from point A to point B.

Consolidates it

Freight Forwarder

Arranges transport on behalf of a buyer or seller, often combining small shipments into one and usually working multimodal routes.

Side by side

Broker vs. Freight Forwarder

A broker mainly finds the right carrier and negotiates the deal. A freight forwarder manages more of the shipment — paperwork, consolidation, and coordination from pickup through delivery.

2.2Direct vs. indirect customers

How a customer brings freight to market changes who you deal with and how fast you get paid.

 Direct customersIndirect customers
Logistics dept.Has its own supply-chain team; prefers working directly with carriers.No in-house logistics; relies on brokers / 3PLs.
How loads postAd-hoc bidding or booking platforms, no third party.Posted through brokerages on load boards (e.g. DAT).
Payment speedOften under 30 days.Can stretch to 60–90 days.

2.3Two kinds of broker

Has trucks

Asset-Based Broker

A carrier that also holds brokerage authority. When it can’t cover a brokered load, its own parent fleet can — so it may “cover with its own truck.”

No trucks

Non-Asset Broker

Starts as a pure broker, growing on sales and referrals. Must keep a strong carrier database to cover loads anywhere, anytime.

2.4Carrier: company vs. owner-operator

On the carrier side, the same split from Module 1 applies at the company level.

Full operation

Trucking Company

More trucks and dedicated departments — dispatch, accounting, safety — and it usually provides trucks to its drivers.

One-person shop

Owner-Operator

The driver owns the company; dispatch, accounting, safety, and billing all land on their shoulders — unless they outsource to a carrier for a 10–15% dispatch fee.

2.5How a load — and the money — flows

Follow a typical brokered load. The broker is paid by the shipper and pays the carrier less, keeping the spread.

S
Shipper
Walmart
Deal: $4,000
B
Broker
Arranges load
Keeps spread
C
Carrier
Hauls it
Booked: $3,200
R
Receiver
Consignee
Signs POD

Along the way, paperwork moves with the freight: a signed BOL and a rate confirmation at booking, and a signed BOL / proof of delivery at the end. (Module 7 covers each document.)

2.6When freight gets damaged

Damage is expensive in more ways than one. A dispatcher must control the whole investigation, or it hurts the company.

Consequences of load damage

Damaged freight can mean a bad relationship with the broker, the customer refusing to buy the carrier again, an insurance claim and higher insurance cost, delays on the accounting side, and a long, drawn-out resolution.

2.7Getting paperwork off the road

TripPak Express

A service that lets drivers submit a load’s paperwork by dropping it in a sealed envelope at one of 1,000+ truck-stop boxes nationwide — saving time, storage, and cost. Options range from next-day and 2-day delivery to weekly consolidated pickups.

The Tractor: Anatomy of a Truck

The equipment itself — types of trucks, the parts you’ll name on a call, and whether to rent, lease, or buy.

You don’t need to be a mechanic, but you do need the vocabulary. When a driver says they’re a day cab bobtailing to a shipper, that should mean something to you.

3.1Types of tractor

Trucks split into two families — the semi truck (a tractor that pulls a separate trailer) and the straight truck (cab and cargo box on one frame).

Semi

Sleeper Truck

Has a sleeping compartment attached to the cab, so a driver can run long miles without paying for motels.

Semi

Day Cab

No sleeping area — built for local runs and tight areas where a full tractor is hard to maneuver.

Semi

Expedite Straight Truck

Around 24 ft, built for expedited and long runs — often driven by teams.

Straight

Box Truck

A regular box truck for local, smaller loads.

3.2The major makes

Truck manufacturers you’ll see FreightlinerKenworthPeterbiltVolvoInternationalMack

3.3Exterior parts worth knowing

Parts are grouped by where they sit. You don’t need them all — just enough to follow a breakdown or inspection call.

Front

Front view

Marker / clearance lights, CB antenna, windshield, hood, radiator grill, headlights & high beams, turn signals, bumper, side mirrors (“West Coast mirrors”), tag / plate.

Rear

Rear view

Reflectors, exhaust stack, fifth wheel, air & electric lines, tail lights, mud flaps, utility light.

Side

Side view

Door & window, fairings, catwalk, quarter fenders, front & rear tires and rims, front axle seal, air tanks.

3.4The three supply lines

On the back of the tractor, driver’s side, are three color-coded lines that connect the tractor to the trailer. A driver hooks these before moving the trailer.

Hook-up

Red, green & blue lines

The coiled hoses on the back of the cab: emergency air (red), service air (blue), and electrical (green).

Red, green, blue

Red — air line for the trailer’s emergency brake. Green — the electrical line. Blue — air line for the trailer’s service brake. Start with the blue line, since it’s the farthest away.

RedEmergency / supply air line — charges the trailer’s air and sets the emergency brake.
BlueService air line — applies the trailer brakes when the driver brakes.
GreenElectrical line (the “pigtail”) — powers the trailer’s lights and signals.

3.5A quick word on fuses

Automotive fuses protect a vehicle’s wiring and electrical equipment, generally rated for circuits no higher than 32 volts DC (some systems run 42 V). A blown (“bad”) fuse is a common, cheap cause of an electrical fault on the road.

3.6Rent, lease, or buy

How a carrier puts a truck on the road is an accounting decision as much as a driving one. Each route has trade-offs.

 Lease-to-purchaseRentalPurchase
ProsMinimal down payment; regular maintenance; truck becomes yours once paid off.Almost-new trucks anytime; minimal financial dependency; no added debt; maintained by service.It’s a new truck and fully yours; no return at contract end.
ConsCredit-score hit if payments are late; ties you in.Often older trucks, no sleeper comforts; the most expensive option overall.High down payment; the most expensive financial service up front.

Why lease or rent at all

Leasing and renting let a company avoid being the legal owner, so the truck doesn’t sit on the balance sheet — the cost is posted as an expense instead, which keeps the company from taking on more debt.

Common truck rental & leasing companies PenskeRyderEnterprise Truck RentalU-HaulBudget Truck

Module 4 of 8 · ~14 min

Freight Types

What you’re actually moving — how it’s sold by the truck, classified, and matched to the right trailer.

“Freight” is a catch-all. The skill is reading a load’s type and dimensions and instantly knowing the equipment, the risk, and the rate it should command.

4.1What “freight” really means

Several words get used loosely for the same thing. The shade of meaning matters on paperwork and on the phone.

Goods

Freight

Goods, mostly in the sense of cargo being traded.

Task

Load

A shipment seen as a transportation task — the job to be moved.

Detail

Commodity

The detailed description and origin of the product itself.

Sea

Shipping product

Generally refers to ocean shipping.

Air

Cargo

Generally refers to air shipping.

4.2Sold by the truck: LTL, partial, truckload

The first question on any load is how much of a truck it fills.

Shares a truck

Less-Than-Truckload (LTL)

The most popular type. Your shipment shares a truck with others — the most cost-effective option for small freight.

Medium loads

Partial

A dedicated truck moving fewer loads at once; booked by volume or running feet. Handles all commodity types.

Fills a truck

Truckload (FTL)

Ideal for unpackaged, refrigerated, oversized, or special freight. Not the cheapest, but faster — no transfers.

The LTL trade-off

LTL is cheap but comes with a higher rate per pound, longer transit, and higher damage risk — freight moves through terminals and break-bulks and gets handled repeatedly. Transit time depends on the carrier’s terminal network, not just distance.

As a rough sense of how rate scales with how much of the truck you use, the same lane might run roughly $250–$300 for LTL, $350 for a partial, and $450 for a full truckload.

4.3Freight classification

Beyond size, freight is classified by what it is and how it has to travel. Each class points to a trailer type.

Heavy & over-dimensional limits

Anything past the legal limits needs permits, and extreme loads need an escort.

65′Max length (3′ overhang OK in some states)
8′6″Max width before permitting
13′6″Max height before permits
80,000Max gross weight (lbs)

4.4Hazardous freight (Hazmat)

Anyone transporting hazardous material must comply with Part 172 of the 49 CFR code — which holds the Hazardous Materials Table and the rules on marking, labeling, shipping papers, and placards. Before moving any hazmat, you first determine whether it requires placards, which identify the hazard class. Materials are identified worldwide by four-digit UN numbers.

The nine hazard classes

Class 1

Explosives

Divisions 1.1–1.6 — blasting agents, ammunition, fireworks.

Class 2

Gases

Divisions 2.1–2.3 — flammable, non-flammable, and toxic gases.

Class 3

Flammable Liquid

Gasoline, diesel, solvents, and combustible liquids.

Class 4

Flammable Solid

Spontaneously combustible or dangerous when wet.

Class 5

Oxidizer

Oxidizers and organic peroxides that can intensify fire.

Class 6

Poison (Toxic)

Toxic and infectious substances; inhalation hazards.

Class 7

Radioactive

Radioactive materials requiring strict shielding and routing.

Class 8

Corrosive

Acids and bases that destroy skin, metal, or other freight.

Class 9

Miscellaneous

Other regulated dangerous goods (lithium batteries, dry ice, etc.).

4.5Power-only & deadhead

Tractor only

Power-Only Load

Freight already preloaded on a trailer that just needs a tractor. Drivers also say bobtail — same idea, used as a verb (“I’m bobtailing to the pickup”).

Empty miles

Deadhead

Driving with an empty trailer or no load — e.g. after a drop, heading to the next pickup, a truck stop, or home. Empty miles you generally don’t get paid for.

4.6Doubles, expedited & dedicated lanes

Double / triple (pup) loads

Mostly run by mail carriers — UPS, FedEx, USPS, sometimes Amazon. Freight goes in two short trailers (“pups,” ~26 ft) connected by a dolly, so one pup can be redirected separately.

Expedited / high-value & “straight through”

Expedited means faster transport — sometimes by cargo van or pickup over short, drivable distances. Straight through means the load delivers with no unnecessary stops; long-distance straight-through loads need team drivers.

A dedicated lane is a regular run between two points under a standing contract — e.g. raw material from Richmond, VA to Atlanta, GA every week, with finished goods coming back. Dedicated lanes give consistent gross regardless of the market and high ratings with brokers, but can be short on capacity and hard to cover at peak. Build strong broker relationships to earn access to them.

Load Security & Procedures

Keeping freight from shifting, the gear that loads and unloads it, and the facilities where it all happens.

A load that shifts is a load that gets damaged — and the carrier is usually on the hook. Securing freight and knowing the facility’s rules are core to a clean delivery.

5.1Why load security matters

Load securing (or cargo securing) is fastening cargo for transport so it can’t tip or flip. The carrier is generally responsible for the load’s security in transit — making this the carrier’s problem to get right, and the dispatcher’s to understand.

5.2How freight is secured

Tie-down

Straps

Fasteners that hold cargo down, hitched to side E-tracks and tightened to the load. Some are ratchet (elastic) straps.

Brace

Load Bars (Load Locks)

Square aluminum bars that lock into a trailer’s E-track. Flat-end versions work in trailers without E-tracks.

Brace

Block and Brace

Using lumber to reduce front-to-rear shifting of freight.

Secure

Padlock

A detachable lock that hangs on the trailer doors.

Flatbed

Chains & Binders

A chain plus a device to tighten it — used to secure freight on flatbed and step-deck trailers.

Stabilize

Dunnage Airbags

Airbags placed between pallets to stabilize cargo and fill voids.

Anti-theft

King Pin Lock

A cast-steel lock that covers the king pin to prevent unauthorized hook-ups.

Protect

Blankets

Protect freight from scratches — mostly used when hauling furniture.

5.3Loading & unloading equipment

At the shipper or receiver, a handful of tools do the heavy work.

Lift truck

Forklift

A powered industrial truck used to lift and move materials over short distances.

Manual

Pallet Jack

A hand tool used to lift and move pallets.

Powered

Electric Pallet Jack

A motorized pallet jack for heavier, stacked pallets; some have a platform to ride.

Yard truck

Yard Jockey

A semi-tractor that moves trailers within a yard or warehouse facility.

Interface

Loading Dock

The area of a building where goods vehicles are loaded and unloaded — common at warehouses.

5.4Types of facility

Where you pick up or deliver shapes how the appointment works.

Makes goods

Manufacturing

Essentially a factory with attached storage; light manufacturing ties closely to supply chains (e.g. JIT inventory).

Transfers modes

Terminal

Transfers cargo between modes and buffers it in storage — short dwell for container terminals, longer for bulk.

Holds inventory

Storage

Holds inventory for a period; bulk warehouses store materials like grain or fertilizer.

Throughput

Distribution

Built around moving inventory through quickly — highly integrated into supply chains.

E-commerce

Parcel

Handles large volumes of online orders; many are dedicated e-fulfillment centers.

5.5How facilities operate

Facilities differ in when they load and how they load — both are questions you ask on every booking.

By time

FCFS

First-come, first-serve — trucks accepted by queue, usually in regular working hours.

By time

By Appointment

Trucks scheduled for a specific load/unload time.

By time

24/7

Facility operates around the clock, 365 days.

By procedure

Hook & Drop

For power-only loads — the carrier hooks the vendor’s preloaded trailer.

By procedure

Live Load / Unload

The warehouse loads or unloads while the driver waits on site.

By procedure

Drop Trailer

The carrier drops its own trailer for 24–72 hours to be unloaded.

Safety & Compliance

The agencies, scores, inspections, taxes, and insurance that keep a carrier legal — and on the road.

This is the longest module for a reason: compliance is where dispatchers and brokers get burned. Knowing the agencies, the scores, and the paperwork protects your carrier and your customer.

6.1What safety means here

Trucking is a high-risk profession, and the stakes reach well beyond the cab. A carrier’s safety department exists to reduce crashes, unsafe driving, maintenance problems, and hours-of-service issues — because the safety of the driver and everyone around them comes first.

4,354people died in large-truck crashes in 2023 (U.S.)
65%were occupants of other vehicles, not the truck
16%were truck occupants; 17% were pedestrians, cyclists or motorcyclists
11%of all U.S. motor-vehicle crash deaths that year

The fact that drives everything in this module: in a truck crash, the people most often killed are in other vehicles. Keeping a carrier safe and compliant isn’t paperwork for its own sake — it protects lives. Source: IIHS analysis of NHTSA FARS data, 2023.

6.2USDOT and the FMCSA

The department

US DOT

The US Department of Transportation plans and coordinates federal transportation and sets safety regulations across all major modes. Established in 1966.

The agency

FMCSA

The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, a DOT agency created in 2000, works to improve commercial-vehicle safety and reduce accidents across the trucking industry.

The FMCSA runs two programs you’ll keep meeting: CSA (Compliance, Safety, Accountability), which ranks carriers by safety data, and Hours of Service (HOS), the rules limiting driving hours (and requiring ELDs — see Module 8).

6.3MC vs. USDOT numbers

Carriers and brokers operating across state lines need operating authority and the numbers that go with it.

 USDOT NumberMC Number
Format~7 digits~6 digits
IdentifiesCarriers operating in interstate commerce.A carrier that transports regulated commodities for hire in interstate commerce.

Generally, items changed from their natural state are regulated commodities and require an MC number.

6.4SAFER and CSA

The SAFER portal

FMCSA’s Safety and Fitness Electronic Records (SAFER) system offers company safety data online. You can search carriers, register for a USDOT number, pay fines, order safety profiles, and challenge data via the DataQs system.

The CSA program has three components: Measurement (using inspection and crash results to flag risky carriers), Evaluation (correcting high-risk behavior with tailored interventions), and Intervention (from data collection through enforcement).

6.5The safety score: 7 BASICs

The Safety Measurement System (SMS) organizes data into seven Behavior Analysis and Safety Improvement Categories. Scores update monthly on a rolling 24 months of data.

The seven BASICs Unsafe DrivingHOS ComplianceVehicle MaintenanceDriver FitnessControlled Substances / AlcoholHazmat ComplianceCrash Indicator

Higher is worse

The higher the score in any BASIC, the worse the carrier’s safety record. A score of 95 means 94% of peer carriers have a better record. Brokers must check these before trusting a carrier with a load.

6.6FMCSA safety ratings

After a compliance review (a rated investigation), the FMCSA may assign one of three ratings.

Best

Satisfactory

The carrier has adequate safety-management controls and is complying with federal requirements.

Caution

Conditional

At least one violation found, but no imminent hazard. Financial penalties apply and contractors/insurers may hesitate.

Worst

Unsatisfactory

Serious violations. The carrier must submit an accepted Safety Management Plan within 60 days (45 for passenger/hazmat) or risk being placed out of service.

6.7Compliance reviews & critical violations

A review can be triggered by accidents (even one), repeated out-of-service roadside violations, or failing a New Entrant Safety Audit.

“Critical” or “acute” violations

These cause an immediate unsatisfactory or conditional rating and heavy fines: any drug & alcohol testing violation; using a driver without a valid license or who is medically unqualified; operating without required insurance; failing to keep HOS records; running a vehicle declared out-of-service before repairs; skipping the annual DOT inspection; or falsifying records.

6.8Driver penalties, lightest to heaviest

  1. Oral Warning

    A verbal reminder — doesn’t go on the record or affect the CSA score. Just take action on the issue.

  2. Citation

    The driver is “cited” and ticketed. If convicted or pleading guilty, it stays on the record.

  3. Violation

    Failing a DOT regulation. Sanctions range from written warnings to fines, out-of-service, suspension of operations, or even jail time.

  4. Out-of-Service

    A critical defect stops the driver, vehicle, or cargo until fixed. A mechanical OOS means the truck can’t move until repaired; an ELD/logbook OOS can sideline a driver 10–34 hours.

Driver safety also covers HOS issues, speeding, improper lane changes, harsh driving, no seatbelt, overweight, drug/alcohol records, accidents and claims, document expirations, equipment maintenance, and texting while driving.

6.9The three DOT inspection levels

Level 1

North American Standard

The full inspection — medical certificate, alcohol/drug, log book, seat belt, plus brakes, exhaust, frame, fuel, lamps, steering, suspension, tires, wheels, and more.

Level 2

Walk-Around

Everything in Level 1 except the parts requiring the inspector to go under the vehicle.

Level 3

Driver-Only

An in-depth look at the driver’s license, medical certification, daily log, and signed inspection reports.

6.10Weigh stations, taxes & registration

Trucks stop at weigh stations so states can check weight, brakes, wheels, and driver rest. Skipping a required one can mean being sent back — and extra scrutiny later.

Fuel tax

IFTA

The International Fuel Tax Agreement among 48 US states and 10 Canadian provinces lets carriers report and pay fuel tax with a single license to their base state. Every CMV carries an IFTA sticker.

Credentials

Carrier ID on the truck

FMCSA requires the company name, address, USDOT number, MC number, and truck ID on the side of the tractor. KYU number, GVWR, VIN, and PUC may also appear.

Registration

Cab Card & VIN

A cab card is proof of registration for an apportioned vehicle, carried in the vehicle. The VIN is a unique code identifying the individual vehicle.

Annual

DOT Inspection Decal

A yearly inspection confirms the vehicle meets safety and emissions rules; the decal shows the month and year. Trailer documents live in the nose box.

6.11State mileage permits

Four states want extra

Trucks hauling through Kentucky, New Mexico, New York, or Oregon need specific weight-distance permits. Example: Kentucky (KYU) applies at a declared weight of 59,999 lbs or more; New Mexico applies over 26,000 lbs. If these states are on a regular route, register before you run them.

6.12Insurance & the COI

Freight is high-stakes, so every carrier must carry insurance, shown on a Certificate of Insurance (COI). The main coverages:

Third parties

Automobile Liability

Covers injury or property damage a driver causes to others — not the driver’s own injuries or property. No deductible.

General

General Liability

Broad business liability coverage listed on the COI.

Employees

Workers’ Compensation

Covers work-related injuries and illness — medical bills, lost wages, settlements. Bought as a standalone policy; often required by the state.

Trailers

Trailer Interchange

Covers liability for damage to others’ trailers — common under a trailer interchange agreement, which makes the hauling carrier responsible for damage while in their possession.

Cargo & contingent cargo

Cargo insurance covers loss or damage to the freight. Brokers also carry contingent cargo insurance to pay claims a carrier won’t — it kicks in only when the carrier refuses a claim, and can also cover the gap when a carrier’s cargo limit is too low. It’s not legally required, but carriers are reluctant to work with brokers who lack it.

6.13Screening a driver before hiring: PSP

Beyond watching carriers, the FMCSA gives employers a way to vet individual drivers before hiring. The Pre-Employment Screening Program (PSP), launched in 2010, provides instant access to a commercial driver’s safety record pulled from the federal MCMIS database.

What it shows

5 + 3 years of history

A PSP report contains the driver’s 5-year crash history and 3-year roadside-inspection history, including violations and any out-of-service orders.

The rules

Consent required

An employer may pull a report only with the driver’s written consent (an FCRA requirement), and cannot run PSP on a current employee — it’s strictly for pre-hire screening.

Why it works

An FMCSA study found carriers using PSP to screen new hires cut their crash rate by 8% and their driver out-of-service rate by 17% on average — an estimated 863 crashes and over 3,500 out-of-service incidents prevented in the year studied.

Endorsements, Permits & Legal Documents

The extra permissions a driver needs, the partners who vet carriers, and the paperwork behind every booking.

Some loads need more than a CDL and a clean truck. This module covers the endorsements and permits that unlock freight, the memberships and monitoring services in the industry, and the documents that make a booking real.

7.1Crossing the border

Canada

PARS & documents

The Pre-Arrival Review System (PARS) speeds release of US-to-Canada shipments via a bar-coded cargo-control number. Drivers need Canadian operating authority, a license or passport, and a birth certificate — and must turn on cab lights and open the sleeper for inspection.

Mexico

Documents & forwarder

Requires a shipper’s export declaration, certified BOL, commercial invoice, and (for NAFTA goods) a certificate of origin. A customs broker or freight forwarder typically handles the heavy documentation.

7.2CARB & SCAC

Emissions

CARB Compliance

The California Air Resources Board sets vehicle emissions standards. California is the only state permitted to set its own under the Clean Air Act; others may follow CARB or federal rules. Older heavy trucks must meet a replacement/repower schedule.

Carrier code

SCAC

The Standard Carrier Alpha Code is a 2–4 letter code identifying road-transport companies, developed by the NMFTA in the 1960s. Mostly used by direct customers.

7.3CDL endorsements

Endorsements are “extra permissions” added to a CDL that let a driver operate certain vehicles or haul special goods.

P

Passenger

Allows transporting more passengers than a base CDL permits — may qualify a driver for team-driving jobs.

N

Tanker

Required to haul liquids of any kind. Needs extra training on loading, securing, and handling leaks.

T

Doubles / Triples

Lets a driver pull multiple trailers (two- or three-pup), opening up more job types.

H

Hazmat

Opens many opportunities but requires federal qualification — fingerprints, a background check, and stricter training.

Interstate vs. intrastate

Intrastate carriers trade or transport only within their home state. Interstate crosses state lines — an endorsement available on any class of license, requiring the driver to be at least 21 (a federal rule).

7.4Special-access credentials

Seaports

TWIC Card

A tamper-resistant biometric credential for unescorted access to secure port and vessel areas. Often required at seaport shippers/receivers; without it, an escort fee may apply.

Airports

TSA Certified

Qualifies a driver to pick up or deliver freight at airports, driving up to a passenger/cargo plane for loading.

Other permits & requirements you’ll see Alcohol PermitPPE (safety gear)US Citizenship“No Felonies”

7.5Memberships & partnerships

Drivers

OOIDA

The Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association represents independent owner-operators and professional drivers on issues affecting truckers.

3PLs

TIA

The Transportation Intermediaries Association leads the 3PL industry, serving 1,700+ members on standards and business practices.

Green

SmartWay

A US-government partnership encouraging businesses to manage logistics in an environmentally responsible way.

7.6Carrier monitoring

Monitoring services protect brokers from using unqualified, non-compliant, or unsafe carriers, and act as databases where brokers report carrier conduct (e.g. Carrier411, SaferWatch).

What gets a carrier reported

Double brokerage, unsafe driving, deceptive practices, holding a load hostage, cancelling after accepting, no-show / no-call, back-soliciting the shipper, modifying an agreement in transit, theft or unjustified loss of freight, and persistent cancelling.

7.7The carrier setup packet

Before a broker and carrier do business, the broker sends a Carrier Setup Packet to establish the relationship, prove legality, and collect key information. The carrier fills it out and attaches documents.

Carrier fills outCarrier providesBroker provides
Carrier information & equipmentW-9W-9
Pay options & questionnaireOperating AuthorityOperating Authority
Carrier-Broker AgreementCertificate of InsuranceCertificate of Insurance
 Notice of Assignment (bond)Other requested documents

7.8The core documents

Tax

Form W-9

Requests a taxpayer’s name, address, and TIN (SSN or EIN) so a third party can file an information return with the IRS.

Permission

Operating Authority

Government permission to be paid for hauling freight as your own company — issued by the FMCSA as an MC number.

Payment

Notice of Assignment

A letter from a factoring company telling your customers that your receivables are assigned and future payments go to the factor.

Receipt

Bill of Lading (BOL)

The detailed cargo receipt issued at pickup. Once the shipment is complete and signed, it becomes the Proof of Delivery (POD).

Rate Confirmation

A legally binding agreement of pay between broker and carrier. The broker must provide it for the carrier to sign before proceeding — and every detail discussed by phone or email must appear on it.

What the key documents look like

Receipt

Bill of Lading (BOL)

Signed at pickup; becomes the POD on delivery.

Agreement

Rate Confirmation

Legally binding pay agreement — sign and return before dispatch.

Tax

Form W-9

Name, address, and TIN for IRS information returns.

Sample documents for training — field values are examples only.

7.9Accessorial charges

Beyond the flat rate, a carrier can bill the broker for extra services. The most common:

Redo the job

Redelivery

Charged when a delivery can’t be accepted or is rejected — one of the priciest, since it makes the carrier repeat the trip.

Labor

Lumper / Driver Load-Unload

Charged when the driver must load or unload, which is outside the general job.

Fuel

Fuel Surcharge (FSC)

Added according to the current price of fuel.

Cancelled

TONU

Truck Ordered Not Used — charged if a truck is cancelled after a pre-set cut-off time.

Extra stops

Additional Stops

When a shipment has two or more destinations requiring several stops.

Waiting

Detention & Layover

Detention applies when a driver is held past allowed time at a shipper/receiver; layover when the truck can’t be loaded/unloaded on its delivery day.

Remember

A dispatcher can charge the broker for any extra task not on the rate confirmation — and if the driver had an expense on arrival, the broker must reimburse it. Diversion miles apply if the carrier is sent to a different location on arrival.

Module 8 of 8 · ~10 min
Exit 08

ELD & The Update Department

The device that logs every hour — and the day-to-day work of booking, tracking, and updating a load.

The final stretch: how driving hours are logged and enforced, and the actual desk workflow — finding loads, negotiating, dispatching, and keeping brokers updated until the POD is signed.

8.1The ELD mandate

The Electronic Logging Device (ELD) mandate is the FMCSA’s effort to improve road safety by accurately recording Hours of Service. Driver fatigue is believed to be the biggest cause of road accidents, and paper logs were easy to falsify — so the ELD automates the record.

From paper to electronic

The old paper logbook had drivers draw lines on a graph for driving, on-duty, and off-duty time — with no proof of action, so falsification was caught by inspectors. ELDs became mandatory by December 16, 2019. If an ELD malfunctions, a driver may use paper logs for up to 8 days.

On the dash

What the driver sees

Every ELD tracks the four clocks dispatchers care about: break, drive, shift (14-hour window), and cycle (60/70-hour limit).

8.2Hours of Service: the real limits

HOS rules (49 CFR Part 395) cap how long a property-carrying driver can work and drive before resetting. There are two clocks every dispatcher watches: the daily limits and the weekly cycle. A driver out of hours can’t legally roll, no matter how close the appointment is.

Two more tools sit on top of the daily clock. A 34-hour restart — 34 or more consecutive hours off duty — resets the weekly 60/70-hour cycle to zero. The sleeper-berth split lets a driver divide the 10 hours off into a 7/3 or 8/2 pairing (at least 7 hours in the berth plus at least 2 more off duty), so neither piece eats the 14-hour window. Adverse driving conditions can extend the driving and window limits by up to 2 hours, and a 150 air-mile short-haul exception covers local drivers who start and end at the same place.

Why it matters on every load

Before promising a pickup or delivery, confirm the driver actually has the hours to make it. Running out of hours is one of the most common reasons a load is late — and an HOS violation can put the driver out of service at a roadside inspection and damage the carrier’s score.

8.3The dispatcher’s job

Performance on the desk is measured by rate per mile, revenue per tractor, trailer utilization, dedicated-lane density, deadhead/empty miles, and load & fuel optimization — all of which ride on effective dispatch, strong relationships, and dependable teamwork.

The dispatch process, step by step

  1. Find & post available trucks

    Check which trucks are ready to roll and post them on your load boards for the available dates.

  2. Source loads

    Use load boards (DAT Power, Truckstop, Truckers Edge, 123Loadboard) to reach brokers, forwarders, and shippers about loads for your equipment.

  3. Negotiate the rate

    Base it on distance, equipment type, freight lane, and hauling area — and the driver’s expectations.

  4. Check credit

    Before accepting, check the broker or shipper’s credit through your factoring or credit service.

  5. Transfer paperwork & insurance

    Complete the carrier-broker agreement and have the broker/shipper added as a Certificate Holder on the insurance.

  6. Sign the rate confirmation

    Review the RC for accuracy, then sign and return it.

  7. Dispatch the driver

    Send pickup/delivery points and times to the carrier — call with the details and email a copy of the RC.

  8. Close out on delivery

    Once delivered, get the signed BOL / POD and paperwork to the broker for payment, all through the TMS.

Tools you’ll live in DATTruckstop123LoadboardPC*MILERProMilesRand McNally

Rate tips & the right questions

Pay attention to the drop-off market (cheap to get into Florida, hard to get out — negotiate higher going in). Get everything in writing — no signed RC, no obligation to pay. Watch the clock: the longer a load sits, the more anxious the broker. And ask up front about the pickup/delivery type (FCFS, appointment, drop trailer), weight and commodity, tolls, permits, lumper fees, detention history, and whether fuel surcharge is included.

8.4The Update Department

The update (track-and-trace) team gives brokers the shipment’s status 24/7, 365 days a year. It calls for excellent communication, multitasking, quick judgment, problem-solving, and formal writing.

Watching a load to pickup

After the dispatch message goes to the driver, the team confirms the ETA to pickup, finds the truck’s location and measures distance (figuring ~50 mph), checks that an empty trailer is attached (or that the driver is bobtailing for a power-only), verifies the driver is rolling and has enough hours, leaves a note with location and mileage, then checks again 30 minutes before the appointment and confirms the driver checked in at the right place.

Watching a load to delivery

After a clean pickup, the team confirms it was on time and the trailer is now loaded, calculates transit time to the consignee’s appointment (~50 mph), gets the driver’s ETA, leaves a note, checks every 1–2 hours that the driver is on pace, and finally arrives the load in the system from the delivery check-in/out times.

Common reasons for delay TrafficMechanical issuesStuck unloading at previousStuck loading at shipperDriver health

8.5Updating brokers: email & phone

Email updates

Always formal English — no “hey buddy” or “dude.” Always include the load / reference number. Answer exactly what’s asked without burying it in extra information: driver info, ETA to pickup/receiver, in/out times, location updates, delivered info, and the POD.

Phone updates

Greet the caller and name the company, listen carefully while finding the info in the system, provide what they need, confirm there’s nothing else, thank them, and leave a note that the broker was updated by phone.

You made it to the end of the route

That’s the full loop — from who’s behind the wheel to a signed POD. Keep the glossary handy on the job, and revisit any exit on the route whenever you need a refresher.

REF

Glossary

The working vocabulary of the dispatch desk — every term a broker or dispatcher runs into on the job.

129 terms
ABCDEFHIJKLMNOPRSTVWY
Accessorial Charge
Amount billed for additional, supplemental, or special services provided, usually a flat fee. Examples: tarps, dunnage, layovers, detention.
All-in Line Haul
The full per-mile rate including fuel: Fuel Surcharge (FSC) + Line Haul.
Authority
The license every trucking company must have to transport freight in the US. The type (Common/Contract or Brokerage) shows how freight is moved; found via the company's MC number.
Axles
Structural component to which wheels, brakes, and suspensions attach. DOT law caps the weight each may carry: Steer 12,000 lbs, Drive 34,000 lbs, Trailer 34,000 lbs.
Backhaul
The return movement of a vehicle from its delivery point back toward its point of origin. Traditionally cheaper than a head haul.
Bill of Lading (BOL)
Paper document between shipper and carrier acknowledging receipt of goods for transport. Describes the cargo's nature, weight, size or piece count, and origin and destination.
Block and Brace
A method of securing freight against movement in transit using load locks, bars, straps, or 2x4s nailed to the trailer floor.
Bobtail
Driving a semi-tractor without a trailer attached.
Booking
The process of assigning a carrier to a load; also called selling a load to a carrier.
Broker (Freight)
Individual or company that acts as liaison between a shipper needing transport and an authorized carrier, connecting the two at an acceptable price.
Cab
The driver's compartment of a truck or tractor.
Cargo Van
A van tall enough to clear pallets and reach dock level; typically hauls 1-2 pallets, often used for expedited freight.
Carrier
Uses trucks and/or trailers to move goods from point A to point B.
CDL
Commercial Driver's License. Authorizes an individual to operate commercial motor vehicles and buses over 26,000 lbs gross vehicle weight.
Chains
Used to secure freight to a flatbed trailer, running from side to side and tightened across. Different chains may also be used on tires in snow. See Straps.
Claim
In insurance, a request filed by a company that suffered a loss from an OS&D (Overage, Shortage, or Damage) issue.
Clean BOL
A BOL signed by carrier and consignee confirming merchandise received in good condition, with no apparent damage or loss. Clean bills mean no issues with the load.
Coil Racks (Bed Rolls)
Prefabricated wood or steel cradles made to hold rolled coils and keep them from rolling on a trailer.
Comcheck
A numbered code given to carriers that can be cashed like a check at most truck stops.
Commodity
Any article of commerce, including raw material and manufactured or grown products.
Consignee
The person or location to whom a shipment is delivered, whether by land, sea, or air.
Cross-Dock
Moving freight from one truck to another, usually at a warehouse but also by backing two trailers together and shifting freight between them.
Curtain Side Trailer
A van whose walls are tarp-like material rather than metal or wood.
D.O.T. Number
License administered to for-hire carriers by the Department of Transportation. Not the same as a Motor Carrier number.
DAT
An online load board (DAT.com) where shippers and carriers post available loads and trucks.
Day Cab
A tractor without a sleeper compartment, usually used for local freight and tight areas where standard tractors are hard to maneuver.
Dead-Head
The distance a driver must drive an empty truck to reach the next load.
Dedicated Run
A load that ships regularly and is promised to one carrier (and sometimes one driver) to haul.
Dedicated Team
A team of drivers who take turns driving a dedicated truck.
Dedicated Truck
A truck pulling freight for one specific customer only; no partial loads added.
Department of Transportation (DOT)
Oversees US federal highway, air, railroad, maritime, and other transportation functions.
Detention / Demurrage
A carrier charge for excess retention of their equipment, typically from untimely loading or unloading.
Dispatcher
A person at a carrier responsible for dispatching and planning loads for drivers.
Distribution Center (DC)
A location where goods and materials are stored until ready to move to their end destination.
Dock
An elevated loading/unloading area at a warehouse, level with the back of a trailer, so forklifts can drive on and off.
Double Drop
A flatbed with the lowest deck, normally used for oversized or over-height loads.
Drop and Hook
Taking an empty trailer into a shipper, dropping it, and later picking it up loaded. Saves time and reduces dock waiting.
Dry Van
A 48' or 53' enclosed trailer with wooden walls and floors.
ETA
Expected Time of Arrival; the approximate time a truck will reach a pickup or destination.
Expedited
Shipping at a faster rate than normal, usually with team drivers, overnight, or air services.
FAK
Freight of All Kinds; a generalization for general freight, used when a shipment contains many different products.
Food Grade Trailer
A van or reefer clean enough to haul food products, free of odors and certain prior commodities. Shippers inspect and reject trailers that don't qualify.
Freeze Protect
A directive from shippers of freezable product (e.g. bottled beverages) to protect it during cold temperatures.
Freight Class
In LTL, the category of freight defined by the National Motor Freight Traffic Association, based on size, value, and difficulty of transport. Determines shipping charges.
Fuel Surcharge (FSC)
An additional charge added to the line-haul rate to cover fuel cost. Fluctuates with the national average fuel price each week.
Hazmat
Hazardous materials as classified by the EPA. Transport is strictly regulated by the US DOT.
Head Haul
Loads going outbound from a carrier's home base. Traditionally more expensive than a backhaul.
Heated Van
A dry van with a heating unit, used when a product can't move on a reefer but must be kept warm.
Heavy Weight
The total weight of truck + trailer + load, also called Gross Combination Weight (GCW). Cannot exceed 80,000 lbs.
High Cube
A taller trailer (110" high). By definition it must have swing doors.
High Risk Freight
A load of electronics, pharmaceuticals, liquor, or precious metal; or a load over $100,000 of apparel, cosmetics, beer, or wine.
High Value Freight
A load valued over $100,000 that does not consist of electronics, pharmaceuticals, liquor, precious metal, apparel, cosmetics, beer, or wine.
Hot Load
A high-profile or expedited load.
Hot Shot
Smaller trailers (24-40') pulled by larger pickups; can't carry as much as a tractor-trailer. Common for small loads and LTL.
Hours of Service (HOS)
Federal regulations limiting when and how long drivers may drive.
Interchange Agreement
A contract between two companies to switch or take control of a trailer for pickup and delivery. Common at the Mexico-US border.
Intermodal
A single trailer or container that uses multiple modes of transport along its route, such as truck/ship or truck/rail.
Interstate Loads
Loads shipping from one state to another (e.g. TX to PA).
Intrastate Loads
Loads shipping within the same state (e.g. TX to TX).
Just in Time (JIT)
A manufacturing system relying on frequent, small deliveries of parts and supplies to keep on-site inventory minimal.
Kick Plate
A metal plate at the base of a door or panel to protect it from wear. May run along a trailer's interior floor and reduce interior width.
Kingpin
A vertical bolt that joins the tractor to the trailer and acts as the pivot between them.
Lane
A move from point A to point B. A regularly run lane is called a dedicated lane.
Layover
When a driver is held overnight or for a 24-hour period while waiting to pick up or deliver. Fees usually apply.
Less-Than-Truckload (LTL)
A quantity of freight less than a full truckload rate requires. Carriers often combine several LTL shipments on one truck to reduce cost.
Lift Gate
A power-operated tail gate that lifts pallets from street level to trailer-floor level. Used where there's no dock; common on LTL fleets.
Light Weight
The weight of an empty truck + trailer, with no load.
Line Haul
The per-mile rate, in dollars and cents, for transporting items.
Load
A shipment of freight moving from point A to point B.
Load Lock
A removable pole or bar spanning a trailer's width to keep freight from shifting in transit.
LOT (Loaded Out Trailer)
A trailer that has been loaded at the shipper and is ready to roll or already in transit — the opposite of an empty trailer at pickup.
Logbooks
Books in which drivers record their hours of service and duty status for each 24-hour period. Required for interstate trucking by the US DOT.
Logistics Van
A van equipped with E-Track racking, allowing multiple rows of cargo to be loaded inside.
Lumper
A worker at a warehouse a driver may hire to unload the truck. The carrier is paid and the customer charged as an accessorial, with a receipt.
MABD
Must Arrive By Date; for shipments required to deliver by a specific date.
Milk Run
Any load with more than three stops.
Motor Carrier Number (MC#)
License administered to for-hire carriers by the FMCSA, used alongside the USDOT number.
Multi-Drop
Any load with more than one delivery.
Multi-Pick
Any load with more than one pickup.
National Motor Freight Classification (NMFC)
A standard comparison of commodities in commerce, with 18 classes based on density, stowability, handling, and liability.
Over-Dimensional (Wide Load)
Cargo larger than legal limits for width, length, height, or weight that can't be broken into smaller units.
Owner-Operator
A truck driver who owns and operates their own truck(s).
Pallet
A platform, usually wood, on which merchandise is stacked for forklift handling. Standard 42"x48" (often 48"x48"); 26 fit on a 53' trailer straight-loaded.
Pallet Exchange
When a shipper/receiver requires the truck to bring in as many like-quality pallets as it ships or receives, keeping pallet inventory stable.
Pallet Jack
A tool used to lift and move pallets and other heavy products.
Partial
A truck compiling multiple shipments from several customers to use the whole truck; transit times run longer due to multiple stops.
Pick Ticket
An order confirmation from a customer to a warehouse, indicating exactly what to pull and ship.
Placard
Warning signs placed on all four sides of a trailer to denote hazardous materials.
Power Only Moves
A load where only the tractor is required, because the customer has its own preloaded trailers.
Power Unit
Another term for the truck or tractor.
Prepaid
Freight charges paid by the shipper. Abbreviated ppd.
Private Carrier
A business that operates trucks mainly to transport its own products; transportation is not its principal activity.
Proof of Delivery (POD)
Signed documents (usually a BOL) showing a shipment was received at the delivery location.
Pup Trailer
A short semitrailer, usually 26'-32' long, with a single axle.
Ramps
Carried by some open-deck truckers to help load and unload; mostly on step decks hauling cars or drivable equipment.
Rate
The charge for transporting freight, either line-haul (A to B before fuel) or all-in (line-haul + fuel).
Rate Confirmation
A document confirming the agreed cost of service between shipper/broker and carrier.
Recyclable Freight
Baled plastics, scrap metal, and similar; not recommended for a food-grade trailer.
Reefer
A trailer with insulated walls and a self-powered refrigeration unit, most commonly used for food.
Removable Goose Neck (RGN)
A heavy-haul flatbed whose deck attaches to a gooseneck that lowers and detaches, allowing drive-on/drive-off loading.
Roll
To change a load's pickup from the current day to the next (e.g. pick Monday becomes pick Tuesday), often from tight capacity or no carrier.
Roll Doors
Truck doors that roll up like a garage door; they reduce interior height, making some freight impossible to load.
Scale
The total weight a truck can legally haul. A two-axle loaded truck can't exceed 80,000 lbs; most scale between 42,000 and 46,000 lbs.
Seal
A plastic tie placed on a locked trailer once loading is complete, with a unique number recorded on the BOL. An intact seal at delivery means the freight was undisturbed.
Shipper
The consignor, exporter, or seller named in the bill of lading, who may or may not initiate the shipment.
Skid
Another term for a pallet.
Sleeper Cab
A tractor with an area designed for sleeping.
Sliding Tandem
A mechanism that moves a tandem-axle suspension back and forth at the rear of a semitrailer to adjust weight distribution.
Slip Sheet
A plastic or cardboard sheet placed under product on the trailer floor to protect it and save pallet height for more space.
Spread Axle (Spread Tandem)
A tandem-axle assembly spaced wider than the standard 54" spacing.
Straps
Strong vinyl straps used to secure and tie down freight to a trailer.
Surcharge
A charge above the usual or customary charge.
Swing Doors
Trailer doors that swing open (vs. roll-up). They allow taller pallets and forklift access and are increasingly standard.
Tailgate
Moving product on a trailer (usually with a pallet jack) from the front to the back, so the warehouse needn't drive a forklift inside &mdash; reducing unload time.
Tandem Axle
A pair of axles and associated suspension located close together.
Tanker
A cylinder designed to haul liquids such as fuel or oil.
Tarps
Often required on flatbeds, step-decks, and uncovered trailers to cover and protect freight; secured with chains or straps.
Team (Driver Team)
Two drivers who alternate driving and resting, typically for expedited shipments at a higher cost.
Third Party Logistics (3PL)
A liaison arranging transport between a company needing shipping and an authorized carrier, providing transport without being the shipper or carrier.
Thru Trailer Service (TTS)
When cargo stays on the same trailer through an international shipment &mdash; the opposite of a trans-load, and generally considered safer.
TONU
Truck Ordered Not Used &mdash; when a shipper cancels after a truck has been dispatched. A fee typically applies.
Totes
Plastic containers similar in size to a pallet, designed to haul liquids or powders.
Tractor
A term used to describe the truck.
Trans-Load
Moving product from one trailer to another to keep a shipment going; standard at international US borders where a carrier can operate in only one country.
Truck-Mounted Crane
A self-propelled loading and unloading machine mounted on a truck body.
Van
An enclosed, boxlike vehicle with rear or side doors used to transport goods.
Vented Van
A standard van with front and rear vents for airflow, typically used for certain produce.
Weight Tickets
Issued at truck scales to determine gross weight. Light tickets are the truck without a load; heavy tickets are with a load. Exceeding 80,000 lbs is illegal.
Y-Split Load
A load where an extra movement is created to accommodate more than one payee &mdash; most often from TONUs or cross-docking.
